title: Research Is Not Informing Decisions
excerpt: Research fails to inform decisions when product teams lack operational evidence, rely on symptom-level evidence, or hold findings that do not answer specific design and prioritisation questions. The result is decision-making driven by opinion, hierarchy, analogy, or incomplete evidence rather than by observed user behaviour under real working conditions.
metaDescription: How product decisions fail when research is absent, symptomatic, or disconnected from operational decisions.
summary: This situation describes the gap between research activity and product decision-making. It distinguishes absence of operational evidence, symptom evidence without causal grounding, and research that exists but does not connect to roadmap, workflow, or design decisions.
definition: Research is not informing decisions when product teams lack direct operational evidence, have only symptom-level evidence, or have findings that do not answer specific design and prioritisation questions.

bodyMarkdown:
## Research that does not reach decisions creates unreliable product direction

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Research is not informing decisions when product teams make roadmap, workflow, or interface choices without operational evidence that explains what users actually do, under what conditions, and where the current design creates friction. In this situation, decisions still happen. The basis shifts to stakeholder opinion, organisational hierarchy, competitive imitation, analogy to adjacent products, or the working assumptions of the people in the room.

The problem is not the existence of opinions. Teams with stronger product instincts may make better opinion-led decisions than teams without those instincts. The problem is reliability. Opinions formed without direct observation of users in operational conditions can reflect the opinion-holder's product context rather than the user's context. A product manager who demos a system in controlled conditions has a different model of difficulty from a field officer using the system under time pressure, variable connectivity, and a queue of waiting clients.

Opinion-led decisions also tend to reflect organisational power. Stakeholders can advocate for what they understand, can measure, or have already committed to. The operational failure modes that determine whether users adopt the product may remain invisible to every person in the decision meeting.

## Three distinct gaps stop research from informing decisions

Research fails to inform product decisions through three structurally different gaps. Each gap requires a different response because each gap produces a different form of uncertainty.

### Absence of operational evidence

Absence occurs when decisions are being made without research grounding because no operational research has been conducted. This is common in products built quickly, in organisations that moved fast to establish market position, and in legacy platforms that predate modern UX research practices.

In absence conditions, the product's architecture reflects the knowledge available when it was built. That knowledge may include reasonable engineering assumptions, stakeholder requirements, and analogies to similar products. The missing knowledge is what users actually do with the product under real working conditions, and why the current design creates friction at the points where it does.

### Symptom evidence without causal grounding

Symptom evidence exists when a team knows that something is wrong but does not know why it is happening. Low adoption metrics, concentrated support tickets, low NPS scores, and user descriptions of a product as difficult all describe effects. They do not identify the causes that decisions require.

A team that knows adoption is low knows it has a problem. It does not know which workflows create friction for which user groups under which conditions. It also does not know whether the barrier is interaction design, information architecture, labelling, training burden, or a combination. Without causal understanding, prioritisation remains assumption-led even when the symptoms are accurately described.

### Research present but disconnected from decisions

Research can exist and still fail to inform decisions when the findings do not answer the questions the product team needs to decide. Abstract usability findings such as users finding navigation confusing do not specify what to redesign. Aggregate satisfaction scores do not distinguish superficial dissatisfaction from operational friction that limits adoption. Survey data about feature preferences reflects what users think they want, not necessarily what would change how they operate the product.

Research in these formats may be cited in roadmap discussions and then set aside because it does not answer the decision question: what specifically should change, in what order, and to what operational end.

## WCO/IPM shows the difference between symptom evidence and causal evidence

The World Customs Organization's IPM platform was already in production and covered an intergovernmental enforcement network spanning most of international trade when Creative Navy was engaged. WCO had symptomatic evidence of an adoption problem: adoption was low across member administrations, officers described the system as difficult to navigate and slow to operate during inspections, and parallel spreadsheets and email chains were running alongside the platform.

The symptomatic evidence did not identify which product decisions would address the adoption problem. The platform had accumulated features and workflows from years of internal product decisions. Some of those features and workflows were contributing to adoption failure, while others were functioning well. Distinguishing between them required direct observation of how inspection officers, analysts, and rights holders operated the system under real field conditions.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used the Sandbox Experiments phase to produce operational evidence through structured observation and research with WCO teams and selected member administrations. The work characterised three user groups operationally: by the tasks they needed to complete, the physical and institutional conditions under which they performed those tasks, and the friction points that produced workaround behaviour.

The research framed adoption issues in operational terms rather than abstract usability language. A general finding that officers find navigation confusing informs discussion. A specific finding that inspection officers processing a shipment during a busy arrival period need to reach historical rights holder data from the active case record without leaving the workflow, and cannot currently do so without four screen transitions, specifies what to change.

The operational framing created a shared view of the problem across WCO operational units, IT teams, and programme leadership. Core inspection workflows and rights holder alert flows were prioritised before secondary features because the research had established that those flows were barriers to adoption.

Client-reported post-redesign outcomes for WCO/IPM were a 200% increase in rights holder sign-ups, a 67% increase in rights holder platform use, a 20% increase in officer platform use, a 78% reduction in officer training costs, and 107 governments signed up to the system. Usability testing with 47 participants from Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain validated the redesigned workflows under realistic conditions. The adoption and training outcomes are client-reported; the usability testing participation is directly observed.

## IDEXX Animana shows why internal knowledge may not be independent evidence

IDEXX Animana was one of the oldest veterinary practice management platforms in Europe, with eleven years of accumulated feature additions, local customisations, and workflow assumptions. Following an acquisition, new leadership wanted an independent, evidence-based assessment of the platform. The issue was not lack of opinion. The issue was that eleven years of internal opinion had produced the current state and could not reliably identify the gaps created by that same perspective.

This is a specific form of the absence problem. Evidence existed as internal knowledge, but that knowledge was compromised as a decision basis because it reflected the perspective that produced the existing design. Internal users who have built and used a product daily can develop a model of the product that differs from the model encountered by a new user. Features that feel natural to experienced internal users may be the same features that created the longest learning curve for users without the design history.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method applied a Sandbox Experiments programme across 35 clinics in the UK, Netherlands, and Germany over two weeks. The research involved 150+ participants across four role types: vets, nurses, reception staff, and administrative staff. Participants ranged from first-week users to ten-year veterans, which allowed Creative Navy to separate learning-curve friction from structural problems embedded in the platform itself.

The research used real-time protocol adaptation. When handwritten workarounds appeared in multiple clinics, including checklists taped to monitors and printed reference sheets near terminals, field protocols were updated during live fieldwork to investigate those patterns in subsequent visits. The workaround material revealed structural failures that users had concluded were not worth reporting.

The central finding was architectural. Two fundamentally different operating modes were sharing a single interface: receptionist multitasking under ambient time pressure and clinical staff working in focused sequential case attention. Eleven years of internal opinion had not resolved the tension because it was not clearly visible from inside the product. It became visible when observed in two different physical environments, under two different time structures, by a team that had developed operational understanding of both roles.

Creative Navy's outputs for IDEXX Animana were a UX audit, four role-based user models, 100+ recommendations structured for direct translation into development tickets, and a five-year product vision with capability stages explicitly linked to research evidence. Six months after the engagement, the client reported that the recommendations were well grounded, with some already implemented and the remainder planned. The research scope is directly observed; the post-engagement status is client-reported.

## Oceaneering shows a research gap named by the client before design began

The Oceaneering engagement illustrates a different pattern: the client identified the research gap at kick-off before design work began. For a hospital dispatch panel redesign, Oceaneering's technology manager identified that no research participants were actual customers. The project lead reported that participants were people with experience of working with customers, not customers themselves.

The reason operators could not be reached was part of the operational condition the design had to address: operators arrive, receive some training, and leave after a few months. A validation plan was agreed at kick-off as urgent. The plan named three targets by role: a hospital logistics manager, someone from the hospital project then in progress, and the external consultants who specify these systems and who also see what competitors are doing.

The Oceaneering case should not be read as a failure illustration. The gap was named by the client, and a plan was made and partly executed. All Oceaneering client speech is reported, not quoted. Only Oceaneering is named; hospital names, product or system names, and individuals are not named.

The sessions that followed in the Oceaneering engagement were design reviews, not usability tests. No task was attempted, nothing was measured, and no dispatch operator took part. The case supports the point that research gaps can be identified constructively before design begins, but it does not support claims about usability testing, comprehension testing, field research, persona development, depot observation, or operator observation.

## Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method turns research into operational decision evidence

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this situation by making research answer causal decision questions in operational terms. Research informs decisions when it establishes what users actually do, under what conditions, to what end, and where the current design produces friction at points that determine whether the product is used or routed around.

Sandbox Experiments are different from standard user research primarily in what the research is trying to establish. Standard user research may establish preferences, satisfaction levels, and the presence or absence of usability problems. Sandbox Experiments establish the operational model: the tasks, conditions, goals, constraints, and friction points that should guide product decisions.

Domain learning is a prerequisite for this work. In the IDEXX Animana engagement, Creative Navy built sufficient working knowledge of veterinary clinical workflows, including consultation patterns, patient intake, lab sample tracking, vaccination management, and multi-pet household administration, to distinguish interface friction from operational constraint. In the WCO/IPM engagement, Creative Navy's understanding of customs intelligence workflows, alert and seizure record logic, and the institutional relationships between officers, analysts, and rights holders made it possible to characterise the operational causes of low adoption.

The structure of Sandbox Experiments is exploratory in scope, adaptive in protocol, and triangulated across multiple evidence sources. This structure produces findings that can drive prioritisation rather than merely inform discussion. When research identifies which users are blocked, under which conditions, at which points in which workflows, the resulting decisions are operational conclusions rather than opinions with evidence attached.

## Boundaries of the evidence on this situation

The WCO/IPM outcomes listed here are client-reported for adoption and training cost changes. The WCO/IPM usability testing participation is directly observed and involved 47 participants from Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain.

The IDEXX Animana research scope is directly observed: 35 clinics in the UK, Netherlands, and Germany over two weeks, with 150+ participants across four role types. The six-month post-engagement implementation status is client-reported.

The Oceaneering material is limited to the research gap identified at kick-off, the validation plan that was agreed, and the design reviews that followed. It does not establish usability outcomes, measured operator performance, comprehension results, field-observation findings, or dispatch-operator evidence.

## Related documentation

This situation is closely related to product teams being unable to prioritise UX work rationally, stakeholders being unable to align on direction, and teams being unable to explain why an experience feels hard. It also relates to products that work in demos but not in real use, high training burden, legacy systems holding back roadmap decisions, and the documented Oceaneering dispatch panel case.
